questiontext.text: In syntax-based testing, a context-free grammar (CFG) is best described as:

answer.text: A finite set of terminals, nonterminals, productions, and a start symbol that together define a language

feedback.text: Correct — those four components define a CFG and the strings it generates.

answer.text: A control-flow graph of a program's basic blocks

feedback.text: That is a CFG in the graph-coverage sense; here CFG means context-free grammar.

answer.text: A table mapping test inputs to expected outputs

feedback.text: That is a test oracle or decision table, not a grammar.

answer.text: A list of mutation operators applied to source code

feedback.text: That is program mutation; a grammar defines a language of strings.

generalfeedback.text: A context-free grammar is the tuple of terminals, nonterminals, productions (rules), and a start symbol; it generates a set of strings called its language.

questiontext.text: A terminal symbol in a grammar is:

answer.text: A symbol that appears literally in generated strings and is never expanded further

feedback.text: Correct — terminals are the atomic tokens that make up the final strings.

answer.text: A symbol that must be replaced using a production

feedback.text: That describes a nonterminal, which is expanded, not a terminal.

answer.text: The single symbol a derivation begins from

feedback.text: That is the start symbol.

answer.text: A rule that rewrites one string into another

feedback.text: That is a production, not a terminal.

generalfeedback.text: Terminals are the literal tokens of the language; they never appear on the left side of a production and are never rewritten.

questiontext.text: A nonterminal symbol in a grammar is:

answer.text: A symbol that stands for a set of strings and is rewritten by productions until only terminals remain

feedback.text: Correct — nonterminals are placeholders expanded via productions.

answer.text: A literal token that appears unchanged in every generated string

feedback.text: That is a terminal.

answer.text: A test requirement produced by a coverage criterion

feedback.text: That is a test requirement, not a grammar symbol.

answer.text: An input that the recognizer must reject

feedback.text: That is a negative test case, not a nonterminal.

generalfeedback.text: Nonterminals (also called variables) are rewritten using productions; a valid string contains only terminals once all nonterminals are expanded.

questiontext.text: A production (rule) of a grammar such as A -> b C specifies:

answer.text: How a nonterminal on the left may be replaced by the string of symbols on the right

feedback.text: Correct — a production is a rewrite rule from a nonterminal to a sequence of symbols.

answer.text: A complete string in the language of the grammar

feedback.text: A production is a rule; a string is the result of applying rules.

answer.text: The starting point of every derivation

feedback.text: That is the start symbol.

answer.text: A terminal that cannot be expanded

feedback.text: A production has a nonterminal on its left and can be applied; terminals cannot.

generalfeedback.text: A production rewrites the nonterminal on its left-hand side into the sequence on its right-hand side; derivations chain productions together.

questiontext.text: The start symbol of a grammar is:

answer.text: The distinguished nonterminal from which every derivation begins

feedback.text: Correct — all derivations of the language start from this symbol.

answer.text: The first terminal in every generated string

feedback.text: The start symbol is a nonterminal, not a terminal of the output.

answer.text: The last production applied in a derivation

feedback.text: The start symbol is where a derivation begins, not a production.

answer.text: Any nonterminal chosen at random for a test

feedback.text: The start symbol is a single distinguished nonterminal fixed by the grammar.

generalfeedback.text: Every derivation of the language starts from the start symbol (often written S); the language is exactly the set of terminal strings derivable from it.

questiontext.text: A derivation in a grammar is:

answer.text: A sequence of production applications that rewrites the start symbol into a string of terminals

feedback.text: Correct — a derivation is the step-by-step rewriting that produces a string.

answer.text: The set of all strings a grammar can produce

feedback.text: That is the language; a derivation produces one such string.

answer.text: A single production of the grammar

feedback.text: A derivation applies many productions in sequence, not just one.

answer.text: A proof that a grammar is ambiguous

feedback.text: Ambiguity is about multiple derivations of one string; a derivation itself is just a rewriting sequence.

generalfeedback.text: A derivation starts at the start symbol and applies productions step by step until only terminals remain; the resulting terminal string is a member of the language.

questiontext.text: Terminal Symbol Coverage (TSC) for a grammar requires that:

answer.text: Every terminal symbol of the grammar appears in at least one test string

feedback.text: Correct — TSC has one test requirement per terminal.

answer.text: Every production of the grammar is used at least once

feedback.text: That is Production Coverage, not Terminal Symbol Coverage.

answer.text: Every possible derivation is exercised

feedback.text: That is derivation (all-derivations) coverage, generally infeasible.

answer.text: Every nonterminal is used as a start symbol

feedback.text: There is one start symbol; TSC is about terminals appearing in tests.

generalfeedback.text: TSC is the weakest grammar criterion: each terminal must appear in some generated/used test string.

questiontext.text: Production Coverage (PDC) for a grammar requires that:

answer.text: Every production (rule alternative) is used in the derivation of at least one test string

feedback.text: Correct — PDC has one test requirement per production.

answer.text: Every terminal symbol appears in at least one test string

feedback.text: That is Terminal Symbol Coverage, which PDC subsumes.

answer.text: Every string of length up to n is generated

feedback.text: PDC counts productions used, not strings of bounded length.

answer.text: Every nonterminal is rewritten exactly once

feedback.text: PDC requires each production to be used, and some may be used many times.

generalfeedback.text: PDC requires each production to be exercised by at least one derivation. Because A -> x | y counts as two productions, both alternatives must be used.

questiontext.text:
Consider the grammar:

S -> a A | b
A -> c | d

How many distinct terminal symbols does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — the terminals are a, b, c, d.
That counts the nonterminals S and A, not the terminals.
Recount — a, b, c, d are four distinct terminals.
That counts terminals plus nonterminals; there are only 4 terminals.

generalfeedback.text: Terminals are the literal tokens on the right-hand sides that are never expanded: a, b, c, d — four in all.

questiontext.text:
Consider the grammar:

S -> a A | b
A -> c | d

How many nonterminals does it have?

feedback.text: Correct — the nonterminals are S and A.
There are two: S and A.
That counts the terminals a, b, c, d, not the nonterminals.
Only S and A appear on a left-hand side; that is two.

generalfeedback.text: Nonterminals are the symbols that appear on a left-hand side and get rewritten: S and A — two in all.

questiontext.text:
Consider the grammar:

S -> a A | b
A -> c | d

Counting each alternative as a separate rule, how many productions are there?

feedback.text: Correct — S -> a A, S -> b, A -> c, A -> d are four productions.
That counts the two lines; each | introduces a separate production, so there are four.
Recount — each alternative counts separately: 2 + 2 = 4.
There are only four alternatives across the two rules.

generalfeedback.text: For Production Coverage every alternative counts separately: S -> a A, S -> b, A -> c, A -> d — four productions.

questiontext.text: In a leftmost derivation, at each step you rewrite:

answer.text: The leftmost nonterminal in the current string

feedback.text: Correct — leftmost derivations always expand the leftmost remaining nonterminal.

answer.text: The rightmost nonterminal in the current string

feedback.text: That defines a rightmost derivation.

answer.text: The leftmost terminal in the current string

feedback.text: Terminals are never rewritten; only nonterminals are expanded.

answer.text: Any nonterminal chosen at random

feedback.text: That is an arbitrary derivation; leftmost fixes the choice to the leftmost nonterminal.

generalfeedback.text: A leftmost derivation expands the leftmost nonterminal at every step; a rightmost derivation always expands the rightmost one.

questiontext.text: In BNF-style notation such as B -> c | d, the vertical bar | denotes:

answer.text: Alternative right-hand sides — B may be rewritten to c or to d

feedback.text: Correct — the bar separates alternative productions for the same nonterminal.

answer.text: Concatenation — B must be rewritten to c followed by d

feedback.text: Concatenation is written by juxtaposition (c d); the bar means choice.

answer.text: Repetition — B may be c repeated d times

feedback.text: The bar means alternation, not repetition.

answer.text: A comment separating documentation from the rule

feedback.text: The bar is part of the grammar syntax, meaning alternation.

generalfeedback.text: The bar is shorthand for separate productions: B -> c | d abbreviates B -> c and B -> d, two productions.

questiontext.text: The language generated by a grammar is:

answer.text: The set of all terminal strings derivable from the start symbol

feedback.text: Correct — the language is exactly the strings the grammar can derive.

answer.text: The set of all productions in the grammar

feedback.text: Those are the rules; the language is the strings they generate.

answer.text: The set of all nonterminals in the grammar

feedback.text: Nonterminals are symbols, not the strings of the language.

answer.text: A single longest string the grammar can produce

feedback.text: The language is the whole set of derivable strings, not one string.

generalfeedback.text: The language L(G) is the set of all terminal strings derivable from the start symbol; a string is "in the language" exactly when some derivation produces it.

questiontext.text: When a grammar is used as a generator in testing, it is used to:

answer.text: Produce (derive) strings to use as test inputs

feedback.text: Correct — a generator applies productions to emit strings for testing.

answer.text: Decide whether a given string is in the language

feedback.text: That is the recognizer role, not the generator role.

answer.text: Compile the grammar into machine code

feedback.text: Generation produces strings, not object code.

answer.text: Count how many productions a program contains

feedback.text: Generation derives strings; it does not analyze a program.

generalfeedback.text: A generator walks the productions to derive valid strings (test inputs); a recognizer instead accepts or rejects a given string.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> a S b | c

Is the string aacbb in the language, and if so which productions derive it?

answer.text: Yes: S -> a S b twice, then S -> c (S => aSb => aaSbb => aacbb)

feedback.text: Correct — two wraps of a...b around a central c gives aacbb.

answer.text: Yes, using only S -> c

feedback.text: S -> c alone derives just "c"; you also need S -> a S b twice.

answer.text: No — the grammar cannot produce two a's

feedback.text: Applying S -> a S b twice produces two a's and two b's.

answer.text: No — c may not appear in the middle

feedback.text: S -> c supplies the central c after the wraps; aacbb is in the language.

generalfeedback.text: The language is a^n c b^n. For aacbb, n = 2: S => aSb => aaSbb => aacbb, using S -> a S b twice and S -> c once.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> a S b | c

Is the string acbb in the language?

answer.text: No — every derivation produces equal numbers of a's and b's, but acbb has one a and two b's

feedback.text: Correct — a^n c b^n forces #a = #b, so acbb is not derivable.

answer.text: Yes, using S -> a S b once then S -> c

feedback.text: That derives "acb" (one a, one b), not "acbb".

answer.text: Yes, using S -> a S b twice

feedback.text: Two wraps give "aa...bb" with two a's; acbb has only one a.

answer.text: No — the grammar cannot produce the terminal b at all

feedback.text: S -> a S b does produce b; the real reason is the a/b counts must be equal.

generalfeedback.text: Each application of S -> a S b adds exactly one a and one b, so any derived string has #a = #b. acbb has 1 a and 2 b, so it is outside the language.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A B
A -> x | y
B -> z | w

What is the minimum number of test strings needed to achieve Production Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. xz and yw together use S -> A B, A -> x, A -> y, B -> z, B -> w.
One string fixes one A-alternative and one B-alternative, so it can use only 3 of the 5 productions.
4 is the number of strings in the language, not the minimum for PDC; two suffice.
5 is the number of productions; a single string can cover several at once, so two strings suffice.

generalfeedback.text: There are 5 productions. Each string chooses one A-alternative and one B-alternative, so at most 3 productions per string. xz and yw cover all 5, so the minimum is 2.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> a S | a

Consider the test set { a }. Which is true?

answer.text: It satisfies Terminal Symbol Coverage but not Production Coverage

feedback.text: Correct — the only terminal a appears, but production S -> a S is never used.

answer.text: It satisfies both TSC and PDC

feedback.text: The derivation of "a" uses only S -> a; S -> a S is uncovered, so PDC fails.

answer.text: It satisfies PDC but not TSC

feedback.text: PDC would require S -> a S too, which "a" does not use.

answer.text: It satisfies neither

feedback.text: The terminal a does appear, so TSC is met.

generalfeedback.text: "a" is derived by S -> a alone, covering the single terminal (TSC met) but leaving the recursive production S -> a S unused, so PDC fails. This shows TSC does not imply PDC.

questiontext.text: Production Coverage subsumes Terminal Symbol Coverage: any test set that satisfies PDC also satisfies TSC.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — using every production forces every terminal (each appears on some right-hand side) to appear.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Every terminal occurs on the right-hand side of at least one production, so covering all productions covers all terminals.

generalfeedback.text: Each terminal appears on some production's right-hand side. Exercising every production therefore uses every terminal, so PDC subsumes TSC (but not conversely).

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A B
A -> x | y
B -> z | w

Which is a correct leftmost derivation of xz?

answer.text: S => A B => x B => x z

feedback.text: Correct — the leftmost nonterminal (A) is expanded before B at each step.

answer.text: S => A B => A z => x z

feedback.text: That expands B (the rightmost nonterminal) first; it is a rightmost derivation.

answer.text: S => A B => x z

feedback.text: This skips a step; each production replaces exactly one nonterminal.

answer.text: S => x z

feedback.text: No single production rewrites S directly to x z; S -> A B must be applied first.

generalfeedback.text: Leftmost means always expand the leftmost nonterminal: S => A B (S -> A B), then A first: => x B (A -> x), then B: => x z (B -> z).

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A B
A -> x | y
B -> z | w

Is yz in the language, and which productions derive it?

answer.text: Yes: S -> A B, then A -> y, then B -> z

feedback.text: Correct — S => A B => y B => y z.

answer.text: Yes: S -> A B, then A -> x, then B -> z

feedback.text: A -> x yields "xz", not "yz"; you need A -> y.

answer.text: No — y and z cannot appear in the same string

feedback.text: A can be y and B can be z independently, so yz is derivable.

answer.text: No — the grammar has no production for y

feedback.text: A -> y is a production, so y is available.

generalfeedback.text: The language is { xz, xw, yz, yw }. For yz: S => A B => y B => y z, using S -> A B, A -> y, B -> z.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A B
A -> x | y
B -> z | w

How many test requirements does Terminal Symbol Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — one requirement per terminal: x, y, z, w.
5 is the production count (for PDC); TSC counts the 4 terminals.
3 is the number of nonterminals (S, A, B); TSC counts terminals, of which there are 4.
Recount — the terminals are x, y, z, w, so four requirements.

generalfeedback.text: TSC has one requirement per terminal symbol. The terminals are x, y, z, w — four requirements.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A B
A -> x | y
B -> z | w

How many test requirements does Production Coverage impose?

feedback.text: Correct — S -> A B, A -> x, A -> y, B -> z, B -> w are five productions.
That counts the three rule lines; each alternative counts separately, giving five.
4 is the terminal count (for TSC); there are five productions.
Recount — 1 (S) + 2 (A) + 2 (B) = 5 productions.

generalfeedback.text: Counting each alternative separately: S -> A B (1), A -> x, A -> y (2), B -> z, B -> w (2) = 5 productions, so 5 PDC requirements.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> a S b | c

Which sequence of productions derives acb?

answer.text: S -> a S b, then S -> c

feedback.text: Correct — S => aSb => a c b.

answer.text: S -> c only

feedback.text: S -> c alone derives just "c", not "acb".

answer.text: S -> a S b, then S -> a S b

feedback.text: Two wraps give "aa...bb"; you need S -> c to finish "acb".

answer.text: S -> a S b, then S -> a S b, then S -> c

feedback.text: That derives "aacbb", not "acb".

generalfeedback.text: acb needs one wrap and then the central c: S => aSb (S -> a S b) => a c b (S -> c). This single string already exercises both productions of the grammar.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

E -> E + T | T
T -> a | b

What is the minimum number of test strings needed to achieve Production Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — a+b uses all four productions: E -> E + T, E -> T, T -> a, T -> b.
Two are not needed: the single recursive string a+b already exercises every production.
One string suffices; a+b covers all four productions.
4 is the production count; one well-chosen string can hit all of them.

generalfeedback.text: Derive a+b leftmost: E => E + T (E -> E + T) => T + T (E -> T) => a + T (T -> a) => a + b (T -> b). All four productions are used, so one string achieves PDC.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A B
A -> x | y
B -> z | w

Which production is left uncovered by the test set { xz, xw }?

answer.text: A -> y

feedback.text: Correct — both strings begin with x, so A -> y is never used.

answer.text: B -> z

feedback.text: xz uses B -> z, so it is covered.

answer.text: B -> w

feedback.text: xw uses B -> w, so it is covered.

answer.text: S -> A B

feedback.text: Both strings use S -> A B, so it is covered.

generalfeedback.text: { xz, xw } uses S -> A B, A -> x, B -> z, B -> w but never A -> y. So PDC is not met (and, incidentally, the terminal y is never generated).

questiontext.text: A test set can satisfy Terminal Symbol Coverage without satisfying Production Coverage.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — TSC does not subsume PDC; e.g. for S -> a S | a the set { a } meets TSC but not PDC.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Subsumption runs only one way: PDC implies TSC, but TSC does not imply PDC.

generalfeedback.text: PDC subsumes TSC, not the reverse. A terminal may be reachable through a production that a TSC-satisfying set never exercises, leaving PDC unmet.

questiontext.text: A recognizer built from a grammar is used to:

answer.text: Decide whether a given input string is in the language (accept or reject it)

feedback.text: Correct — a recognizer parses an input and reports membership.

answer.text: Derive new strings to serve as test inputs

feedback.text: That is the generator role, not the recognizer role.

answer.text: Count the number of productions in the grammar

feedback.text: A recognizer classifies strings; it does not count rules.

answer.text: Mutate the grammar to create invalid strings

feedback.text: That is grammar mutation; a recognizer only accepts or rejects.

generalfeedback.text: A recognizer answers "is this string in L(G)?" by accepting or rejecting; a generator instead emits strings. The same grammar can back both roles.

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

E -> E + T | T
T -> a | b

Is the string a+b+a in the language?

answer.text: Yes — apply E -> E + T twice, then E -> T, then T -> a, T -> b, T -> a

feedback.text: Correct — E => E+T => E+T+T => T+T+T => a+b+a is derivable.

answer.text: No — the grammar allows at most one + per string

feedback.text: E -> E + T is recursive, so any number of + operators is allowed.

answer.text: No — the grammar cannot produce the terminal a twice

feedback.text: T -> a can be applied at more than one position, so a may occur repeatedly.

answer.text: Yes, but only using T -> a (never T -> b)

feedback.text: The middle operand is b, so T -> b is needed; both a and b appear.

generalfeedback.text: E -> E + T is left-recursive, so E => E+T => (E+T)+T => (T+T)+T => a+b+a. The recursion permits arbitrarily many + operators.

questiontext.text: Covering every possible derivation of a grammar (all-derivations coverage) is generally infeasible because:

answer.text: Recursive productions allow infinitely many derivations, so the requirement set is unbounded

feedback.text: Correct — this mirrors why complete path coverage is infeasible with loops.

answer.text: Grammars have no start symbol to begin derivations

feedback.text: Every CFG has a start symbol; that is not the problem.

answer.text: Terminals cannot be distinguished from nonterminals

feedback.text: They are clearly distinguished; recursion, not confusion, causes the blow-up.

answer.text: Production Coverage already forbids more than one derivation

feedback.text: PDC places no such limit; the issue is the unbounded number of derivations.

generalfeedback.text: A recursive production (e.g. E -> E + T) can be applied any number of times, yielding infinitely many derivations — analogous to loops making complete path coverage infeasible.

questiontext.text:
Original grammar:

S -> a S b | c

You mutate the production S -> c into S -> d, giving the mutant S -> a S b | d. Which string does the mutant derive that is not in the original language (a valid negative test)?

answer.text: aadbb

feedback.text: Correct — the mutant derives a^n d b^n; aadbb is outside the original a^n c b^n.

answer.text: aacbb

feedback.text: aacbb is in the original language, so it is a valid input, not a negative test.

answer.text: acb

feedback.text: acb is in the original language; the mutant no longer derives it, and it is not a negative test.

answer.text: aadb

feedback.text: aadb has two a's but one b, so neither grammar derives it; it is not a mutant string.

generalfeedback.text: The mutant language is a^n d b^n. aadbb (n = 2) is derivable by the mutant but not by the original, so it is exactly the kind of invalid input used to test error handling.

name.text: Minimal PDC set with a top-level choice

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A | B
A -> a A | a
B -> b

What is the minimum number of test strings needed for Production Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. aa (covers S -> A, A -> a A, A -> a) and b (covers S -> B, B -> b).
One string picks either S -> A or S -> B, so it cannot cover both top-level alternatives.
Two strings suffice: "aa" and "b" together use all five productions.
5 is the production count; strings cover several productions each, so two suffice.

generalfeedback.text: There are 5 productions. "aa" gives S -> A, A -> a A, A -> a; "b" gives S -> B, B -> b. Because S -> A and S -> B are mutually exclusive in one derivation, no single string can do both, so the minimum is 2.

name.text: Which string is outside the language

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> a S b | c

Which string is not in the language (so a parser should reject it)?

answer.text: aabb

feedback.text: Correct — every string in the language contains exactly one central c; aabb has none.

answer.text: aacbb

feedback.text: aacbb = a^2 c b^2 is in the language.

answer.text: acb

feedback.text: acb = a^1 c b^1 is in the language.

answer.text: c

feedback.text: c is derived directly by S -> c, so it is in the language.

generalfeedback.text: Every derivation ends by applying S -> c, so each string has exactly one c in the middle. aabb has no c and is therefore outside the language.

name.text: Generator and recognizer in test generation

questiontext.text: In grammar-based testing you want to produce valid inputs and also decide whether the system under test classifies them correctly. Which pairing of roles is right?

answer.text: Use the grammar as a generator to derive inputs; use a recognizer as an oracle to check acceptance/rejection

feedback.text: Correct — generator produces strings, recognizer decides membership.

answer.text: Use the grammar as a recognizer to derive inputs; use a generator to reject them

feedback.text: The roles are swapped: recognizers decide membership, generators produce strings.

answer.text: Use mutation operators to both derive and classify inputs

feedback.text: Mutation creates invalid variants; it is not how valid inputs are generated or classified.

answer.text: Use Production Coverage to derive inputs and Terminal Symbol Coverage to reject them

feedback.text: Those are coverage criteria, not the generator/recognizer mechanisms.

generalfeedback.text: A generator walks the productions to emit strings (test inputs); a recognizer parses a string and answers whether it is in the language, acting as the oracle for valid/invalid classification.

name.text: Parse trees in an ambiguous grammar

questiontext.text:
Given the ambiguous grammar:

E -> E + E | a

How many distinct parse trees does the string a+a+a have?

feedback.text: Correct — (a+a)+a and a+(a+a) are the two distinct groupings.
The grammar is ambiguous for this string; there are two distinct parse trees.
Only two ways to parenthesize three operands with one binary operator.
The count is the Catalan number C(2) = 2, not 4.

generalfeedback.text: With three operands there are C(2) = 2 ways to associate the additions: (a+a)+a and a+(a+a). Each yields a distinct parse tree, showing the grammar is ambiguous.

questiontext.text:
Original grammar (language a^n c b^n):

S -> a S b | c

You mutate S -> a S b into S -> a S b b. Which string is derivable by the mutant but rejected by the original (a good negative test)?

answer.text: acbb

feedback.text: Correct — S => a S b b => a c b b; a^1 c b^2 is not in the original a^n c b^n.

answer.text: c

feedback.text: c is derivable by both grammars (S -> c), so it is not a negative test.

answer.text: acb

feedback.text: acb is in the original language, but the mutant (with S -> a S b b) cannot derive it, so it is not a mutant string.

answer.text: aabb

feedback.text: aabb has no c, so neither grammar derives it.

generalfeedback.text: The mutant derives a^n c b^(2n). acbb (n = 1) is derivable by the mutant but has unequal a/b counts, so the original rejects it — exactly a negative test for error handling.

name.text: Minimal PDC set for if-then grammar

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar (treat if, then, s, t, f as terminals):

S -> if C then S | s
C -> t | f

What is the minimum number of test strings needed for Production Coverage?

feedback.text: Incorrect — this assumes C -> t and C -> f cannot both occur in one derivation, but the recursion lets both occur in a single nested string such as "if t then if f then s", so one test suffices.
Correct — S is recursive (S -> if C then S), so one nested string like "if t then if f then s" covers all four productions: two uses of S -> if C then S, plus C -> t, C -> f, and S -> s.
Two suffice: the two strings above cover S -> if C then S, S -> s, C -> t, C -> f.
4 is the production count; a single string covers several productions, so two suffice.

generalfeedback.text: Four productions: S -> if C then S, S -> s, C -> t, C -> f. Because S is recursive (S -> if C then S), a single nested string such as "if t then if f then s" uses S -> if C then S twice plus C -> t, C -> f, and S -> s — all four productions in one string. So the minimum is 1.

name.text: Mutation to accept an invalid string

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A B
A -> x | y
B -> z | w

The string xy is not in the language. Which single production mutation makes xy derivable (turning it into a mutant-accepted invalid input)?

answer.text: Change B -> w to B -> y

feedback.text: Correct — then S => A B => x B => x y using A -> x and the mutated B -> y.

answer.text: Change A -> y to A -> x

feedback.text: That removes an A-alternative; it does not let B produce y, so xy stays underivable.

answer.text: Change S -> A B to S -> B A

feedback.text: Then strings are (z|w)(x|y); xy (x then y) is still not derivable.

answer.text: Change A -> x to A -> x y

feedback.text: Then A can be "xy" but S -> A B still appends a B, giving xyz or xyw, not "xy".

generalfeedback.text: xy needs A to give x and the second symbol to be y. Making B -> y (from B -> w) lets S => A B => x B => x y. The mutant now accepts an invalid input, useful for negative testing of the recognizer.

questiontext.text: Covering every derivation of a grammar with recursive productions is generally infeasible, for the same reason that Complete Path Coverage is infeasible on a graph with a loop.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — recursion in a grammar plays the role a loop plays in a graph: infinitely many possibilities.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: A recursive production can be applied arbitrarily often, giving unboundedly many derivations, just as a loop gives unboundedly many paths.

generalfeedback.text: Recursion is the grammar analogue of a loop: both create an unbounded set of possibilities, so covering all of them (all derivations / all paths) cannot be finitely satisfied.

name.text: Count strings up to a length

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> a S b | c

How many distinct strings of length at most 5 are in the language?

feedback.text: Correct — c (length 1), acb (length 3), aacbb (length 5).
There are three: lengths 1, 3, and 5 (n = 0, 1, 2).
The next string, aaacbbb, has length 7, which exceeds 5.
Only n = 0, 1, 2 give lengths 1, 3, 5 within the bound; that is three strings.

generalfeedback.text: A string a^n c b^n has length 2n + 1. Length at most 5 means 2n + 1 <= 5, i.e. n <= 2: c, acb, aacbb — three strings.

questiontext.text:
Original grammar (language a^n c b^n):

S -> a S b | c

You mutate S -> a S b into S -> a S. Which string becomes derivable by the mutant that was not in the original language?

answer.text: aac

feedback.text: Correct — the mutant derives a^n c; S => a S => a a S => a a c, which the original never produces.

answer.text: aacbb

feedback.text: aacbb is in the original language, and the mutant (no b) cannot produce it at all.

answer.text: acb

feedback.text: acb is in the original language; the mutant has no b, so it cannot derive it either.

answer.text: abc

feedback.text: The mutant produces a^n c (no b), so abc is not derivable by it.

generalfeedback.text: Dropping the trailing b changes the language to a^n c. aac (n = 2) is now derivable but is not in the original a^n c b^n, so it is a negative test for the recognizer.

name.text: Leftmost derivation on a recursive grammar

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

E -> E + T | T
T -> a | b

Which is a correct leftmost derivation of a+b?

answer.text: E => E + T => T + T => a + T => a + b

feedback.text: Correct — the leftmost nonterminal is expanded at each step (E, then the inner E, then the T's left-to-right).

answer.text: E => E + T => E + b => T + b => a + b

feedback.text: That expands the rightmost T before the left E; it is a rightmost derivation.

answer.text: E => E + T => a + T => a + b

feedback.text: The leftmost symbol after step 1 is the nonterminal E, not a T; you cannot rewrite it to "a" without first applying E -> T.

answer.text: E => T => a

feedback.text: That derives just "a"; it never produces the + operator.

generalfeedback.text: Leftmost always expands the leftmost nonterminal: E => E + T (E -> E + T); the leftmost E next: => T + T (E -> T); then the T's: => a + T (T -> a) => a + b (T -> b).

name.text: Minimal PDC with three top-level choices

questiontext.text:
Given the grammar:

S -> A | B | C
A -> a
B -> b
C -> c

What is the minimum number of test strings needed for Production Coverage?

feedback.text: Correct — a, b, c each fix a different top-level alternative; all three are needed.
One string uses exactly one of S -> A / S -> B / S -> C, so it cannot cover the other two.
Two strings cover only two of the three mutually exclusive S-alternatives.
6 is the production count; each string covers two productions (one S-alt plus one leaf), so three strings suffice.

generalfeedback.text: There are 6 productions but the three S-alternatives are mutually exclusive per derivation. "a", "b", "c" each cover one S-alternative and its leaf, so exactly 3 strings achieve PDC.

questiontext.text: Why does Production Coverage subsume Terminal Symbol Coverage?

answer.text: Every terminal appears on the right-hand side of some production, so using every production forces every terminal to appear

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly why PDC implies TSC.

answer.text: Because there are always fewer terminals than productions

feedback.text: Counts do not establish subsumption; the reason is that each terminal occurs on some right-hand side.

answer.text: Because TSC and PDC impose exactly the same test requirements

feedback.text: They differ: PDC is strictly stronger, so they are not identical.

answer.text: Because every production contains exactly one terminal

feedback.text: Productions may contain zero or many terminals; subsumption does not depend on that.

generalfeedback.text: A symbol is a terminal of the grammar only if it appears on some production's right-hand side. Exercising all productions therefore generates every terminal, so PDC subsumes TSC; the converse fails.
